column2: A statutory category broader than human individuals
column3: Under the 1961 Act, a company can be a person for tax purposes even though it is not a natural human individual.
column4: Under the 1961 Act, only natural human individuals can be persons for income-tax purposes.

column2: A person within the statutory scope of tax assessment or payment obligations
column3: The statutory assessee concept extends beyond simply identifying someone who earned a salary.
column4: Only a salaried employee can ever be an assessee.

column2: The income-earning period generally preceding its assessment year
column3: Income earned during FY 2024-25 is ordinarily assessed in AY 2025-26 under the 1961 Act.
column4: Income earned during FY 2024-25 is ordinarily assigned to AY 2024-25 under the 1961 Act.

column2: The statutory period associated with assessing the preceding income year
column3: AY 2025-26 generally follows the income period FY 2024-25, subject to special assessment provisions.
column4: Assessment year and previous year under the 1961 Act always denote the same period.

column2: The income period terminology applying from the new Act's commencement
column3: Income earned from 1 April 2026 is governed by the 2025 Act's tax-year framework rather than by simply continuing old section numbers unchanged.
column4: The 2025 Act requires every old section number to remain identical after commencement.

column2: The applicable law depends on the income period and transition provisions
column3: The return for FY 2025-26, AY 2026-27, remains governed by the 1961 Act even when filed after 1 April 2026.
column4: Every return filed after 1 April 2026 is automatically governed by the 2025 Act regardless of its income period.

column2: Tax residence determined under statutory tests for a relevant period
column3: Tax residence is not determined solely by citizenship; a citizen can be non-resident under the relevant tests.
column4: Indian citizenship alone automatically makes a person tax-resident for every year.

column2: Residence determined through specified stay conditions with exceptions
column3: For an individual to whom the ordinary tests apply, a stay of at least 182 days in the relevant previous year satisfies one basic residence test under the 1961 Act.
column4: For that ordinary test, a stay of 182 days can never establish residence without an additional 365-day prior-period condition.

column2: The basic combination of current-year and preceding-year stay where applicable
column3: For an individual to whom the ordinary 60-day test applies, 70 days in the current year plus 400 days in the preceding four years satisfies the 60-plus-365 basic test.
column4: Those ordinary-test stays fail the basic test merely because current-year stay is below 182 days.

column2: A residence category whose normal scope includes worldwide income
column3: For an ordinarily resident person, foreign-source income can be within Indian tax scope even without remittance to India, subject to applicable relief and exclusions.
column4: An ordinarily resident person's foreign-source income is automatically outside Indian tax scope until remitted.

column2: A residence category with a qualified scope for certain foreign income
column3: RNOR scope differs from both ROR and NR; relevant foreign income connected with a business controlled in India can matter under the statutory rule.
column4: RNOR and ROR always have identical worldwide-income scope without any qualification.

column2: Tax scope linked to Indian receipt accrual and deemed accrual under applicable rules
column3: A non-resident can be taxable on qualifying Indian-source income without being taxable in India on every unrelated foreign receipt.
column4: Non-resident status automatically exempts every Indian-source receipt from income tax.

column2: The initial receipt distinguished from a later remittance of an already received amount
column3: Remitting a previously received foreign amount to India does not by itself create a fresh first receipt of the same income.
column4: Every remittance of already received income becomes a second taxable earning solely because the bank account changes.

column2: Qualifying income from agricultural activity or land under the statutory definition
column3: Rent from qualifying agricultural land situated in India can fall within agricultural income under the statutory conditions.
column4: Rent from every parcel of foreign land automatically qualifies as exempt Indian agricultural income.

column2: Income divided under applicable rules where agricultural and business elements coexist
column3: A mixed operation may require separating agricultural and business components rather than treating all processing income as agricultural.
column4: Every industrial process using a farm product makes all its profit exempt agricultural income.

column2: Using qualifying agricultural income in the specified rate computation for eligible persons
column3: Agricultural income can affect the rate computation where partial-integration conditions apply even though it is not directly included as ordinary taxable income.
column4: Exempt agricultural income can never affect any rate computation in any circumstances.

column2: Exclusion of income distinguished from subtraction under a computation provision
column3: An exemption and a GTI deduction operate at different points in computing total income.
column4: Every exemption and every GTI deduction must be applied at exactly the same computation step.

column2: Aggregate computed income before applicable Chapter VI-A deductions under the 1961 Act
column3: Permitted set-off is considered in arriving at GTI before eligible Chapter VI-A deductions determine total income.
column4: GTI is always computed by deducting all Chapter VI-A amounts before applying any loss set-off.

column2: The taxable income figure after relevant statutory computation adjustments
column3: If GTI is Rs 8 lakh and eligible deductions are Rs 1 lakh, total income is Rs 7 lakh, assuming no special restriction changes those figures.
column4: Those stated figures imply total income Rs 9 lakh.

column2: Income based on an employer-employee relationship under the relevant charging rules
column3: Fees from an independent client do not become salary merely because payments recur monthly.
column4: Every monthly receipt is salary regardless of whether an employment relationship exists.

column2: Salary recognition under the applicable due-or-receipt rules without double taxation
column3: An advance salary amount already taxed on receipt should not be taxed a second time solely when it later becomes due.
column4: Advance salary must necessarily be taxed twice because receipt and due dates differ.

column2: A benefit or amenity within the statutory employment-benefit rules
column3: Non-cash employment benefits may have tax consequences even without an identical cash salary payment.
column4: Only cash payments can ever enter employment-related taxable income.

column2: Tax classification depends on whether the receipt is pension or family pension
column3: Under the 1961 Act, pension received by the former employee is distinguished from family pension received by a beneficiary.
column4: A beneficiary's family pension is always the beneficiary's own employment salary merely because the deceased person was employed.

column2: Tax computation linked to ownership and annual value of relevant buildings or land appurtenant
column3: A tenant subletting a property is not automatically taxed as the owner under house property solely because rent is received.
column4: Every rent receipt belongs to the house-property head regardless of ownership and the actual arrangement.

column2: Gross annual value less qualifying municipal taxes under the applicable rule
column3: With gross annual value Rs 3 lakh and qualifying owner-paid municipal taxes Rs 20,000, NAV is Rs 2.8 lakh.
column4: Those figures give NAV Rs 3.2 lakh.

column2: The statutory thirty-percent deduction from NAV in the relevant historical computation
column3: For the stated 1961-Act case with NAV Rs 2.8 lakh, a 30% standard deduction is Rs 84,000.
column4: That 30% deduction equals the owner's actual repair bills regardless of NAV.

column2: Taxable profits from business or profession after relevant adjustments
column3: Commercial profit must be adjusted for tax disallowances and allowances rather than copied uncritically from accounting profit.
column4: Accounting net profit always equals taxable business income without any tax adjustment.

column2: Deductibility depends on purpose nature and applicable statutory limits
column3: A proprietor's personal holiday cost is not deductible as ordinary business expense merely because paid from a business account.
column4: A personal holiday becomes wholly business expenditure automatically when the business bank account pays it.

column2: A statutory allowance distinct from accounting depreciation
column3: Tax depreciation and book depreciation can differ because their bases and prescribed computation rules differ.
column4: Book depreciation must always equal tax depreciation in every business.

column2: A tax grouping of assets sharing prescribed class and depreciation rate under the historical framework
column3: A block computation can involve opening tax value additions and disposal proceeds rather than depreciation independently chosen for every asset.
column4: A block computation ignores disposal proceeds in every possible case.

column2: Taxable gain arising from qualifying transfer of a capital asset
column3: A gain on transfer must be classified under the relevant asset and tax rules rather than automatically treated as salary.
column4: Every gain from selling a capital asset is employment salary.

column1: Capital asset versus stock in trade
column2: Asset classification affecting the income head and computation
column3: Shares held as trading inventory can give business income rather than automatically the same treatment as investment shares.
column4: All share-sale profits necessarily belong to capital gains regardless of whether shares are trading inventory.

column2: Consideration less permitted costs and exemptions under applicable rules
column3: With consideration Rs 5 lakh, allowed transfer expense Rs 20,000 and allowable cost Rs 3 lakh, the stated gain before exemption is Rs 1.8 lakh.
column4: The same stated amounts give a gain of Rs 2.2 lakh.

column2: Relief depends on the particular provision and qualifying investment or other conditions
column3: Reinvesting sale proceeds does not automatically exempt every gain without checking the applicable provision's conditions.
column4: Any reinvestment of any sale proceeds automatically exempts every capital gain in full.

column2: A residual income head for taxable amounts not chargeable under another specified head
column3: A taxable receipt is examined under its proper head before the residual head is used.
column4: Every receipt may be assigned to other sources even when a specific charging head clearly applies.

column2: Attributing specified income of another person under statutory anti-avoidance rules
column3: A qualifying transfer to a spouse without adequate consideration can require attribution despite formal asset title in the spouse's name.
column4: Changing asset title to a spouse always eliminates every possible attribution rule.

column2: Attribution of specified minor income with statutory exceptions
column3: Under the historical rules, income from a minor's own manual work or qualifying skill has a distinct exception from ordinary passive-income clubbing.
column4: Every rupee earned by a minor from personal skill must always be clubbed without exception.

column2: Attribution distinguishes transferred-asset income from all later independent sources
column3: Under the usual historical clubbing principle, income arising directly from a transferred asset is distinguished from income earned on reinvested accumulated income.
column4: Once an asset is transferred, every later independent income of the transferee is automatically clubbed forever.

column2: Adjustment of eligible losses against eligible income under statutory restrictions
column3: An ordinary business loss cannot be set off against salary under the historical inter-head restriction.
column4: An ordinary business loss can always be set off against salary without restriction.

column2: Capital losses have specified eligible gain categories for set-off
column3: Under the historical rules, long-term capital loss is set off against long-term capital gains rather than ordinary salary.
column4: Long-term capital loss may always be set off against salary.

column2: A loss with special set-off and carry-forward restrictions
column3: A speculation loss has a narrower set-off route than an ordinary non-speculation business loss under the historical rules.
column4: Speculation loss automatically offsets every head of income without restriction.

column2: Future loss relief depends on the type of loss and applicable filing rules
column3: Timely filing requirements apply to specified carried-forward losses, with statutory distinctions for other allowances or losses.
column4: Every loss and allowance has exactly the same filing and carry-forward conditions without exceptions.

column2: A specified deduction group under the 1961 Act with limits and eligibility conditions
column3: Eligibility under historical section 80C depends on the investment or payment and the applicable tax regime.
column4: Every financial investment automatically qualifies for section 80C in every tax regime.

column2: Relevant deductions operate within statutory total-income constraints
column3: A qualifying GTI deduction cannot generally create a negative total income merely because the eligible payment exceeds GTI.
column4: A large Chapter VI-A payment automatically creates a carried-forward negative total income equal to the excess.

column2: Arranging genuine affairs using permitted choices under applicable law
column3: Comparing lawful lease and ownership alternatives is tax planning when the arrangements and deductions are genuine.
column4: Tax planning requires hiding income or creating false invoices.

column2: Unlawful concealment or misstatement to avoid tax
column3: Suppressing genuine taxable sales is distinguished from choosing an allowed statutory deduction.
column4: Suppressing taxable sales is lawful tax planning whenever it improves cash flow.

column2: Arrangements assessed for compliance with law substance and applicable anti-avoidance provisions
column3: A formally structured arrangement can still require anti-abuse analysis rather than being safe solely because documents exist.
column4: Any documented arrangement is immune from every anti-avoidance rule.

column2: Comparing relevant after-tax costs of internal production and external purchase
column3: Using a stated deductible cost Rs 100 and tax rate 30%, after-tax cost is Rs 70 if the deduction is usable.
column4: With those supplied assumptions, after-tax cost is Rs 130.

column2: Comparing relevant after-tax cash flows for asset ownership and leasing
column3: A lease comparison should consider timing and deductible payments, while ownership may involve depreciation and financing effects.
column4: Lease-versus-own decisions need only compare the first month's cash payment.

column2: Evaluating an asset change using incremental after-tax cash flows
column3: Disposal taxes or relief and new depreciation effects can matter in an asset-replacement decision.
column4: Replacement analysis must ignore every tax consequence of disposal and future deductions.

column2: Comparing future avoidable after-tax cash flows from continuing or closing
column3: A fixed historical expenditure does not become relevant merely because the business is considering closure.
column4: Closure analysis must include every historical sunk payment as a new avoidable cash outflow.

column2: The same income facing taxation in more than one jurisdiction under relevant circumstances
column3: Source and residence taxation can overlap, making treaty or domestic relief relevant.
column4: Foreign taxation automatically removes the residence country's taxing rights in every case.

column2: A treaty allocating taxing rights and providing specified double-tax relief
column3: Treaty relief depends on the applicable provisions and eligibility rather than an unconditional exemption for every overseas receipt.
column4: Every DTAA automatically exempts all cross-border income from both countries' tax.

column2: Relief crediting qualifying foreign tax subject to applicable limits
column3: With specified Indian tax Rs 30,000 on the same income and qualifying foreign tax Rs 20,000, a stated capped-credit method permits Rs 20,000 credit.
column4: Under that stated cap, the credit must be Rs 50,000 by adding both taxes.

column2: Pricing related-party transactions under applicable arm's-length rules
column3: Related parties cannot assume that any mutually agreed price is automatically arm's length.
column4: Agreement between associated enterprises alone proves every transaction price is arm's length.

column2: An arm's-length method comparing relevant controlled and uncontrolled prices
column3: Meaningful comparability and suitable adjustments matter when using an uncontrolled price benchmark.
column4: Any unrelated transaction price is automatically comparable regardless of product terms and market conditions.

column2: An arm's-length method starting from resale price and an appropriate gross margin
column3: The resale-price method focuses on an appropriate gross resale margin rather than simply adding a production markup to the supplier's cost.
column4: Resale-price method is identical to adding a markup to manufacturing cost without considering resale price.

column2: An arm's-length method adding an appropriate gross markup to relevant costs
column3: Cost-base comparability and the appropriate markup both matter.
column4: The cost-plus method uses any arbitrary markup without examining comparable functions or costs.

column2: An arm's-length method examining a relevant net profit indicator
column3: TNMM examines a suitable net-margin indicator and comparability rather than treating every firm's gross margin as interchangeable.
column4: TNMM necessarily compares only gross resale margins and never net profit indicators.

column2: Tax deducted at source from specified payments under applicable rules
column3: TDS can be a prepaid-tax credit rather than a separate additional final tax on the same income.
column4: TDS must always be added on top of final tax without giving the recipient any applicable credit.

column2: Tax collected at source on specified transactions under applicable rules
column3: TCS is distinguished from TDS by the applicable collection mechanism and transaction rather than the words being interchangeable.
column4: TDS and TCS necessarily describe the exact same mechanism for every transaction.

column2: Payment of estimated tax liability during the relevant income period under the applicable rules
column3: Advance-tax calculations consider applicable credits and instalment rules rather than waiting automatically until every return is filed.
column4: Advance tax is by definition paid only after final assessment has concluded.

column2: Tax paid toward remaining liability when completing the relevant return computation
column3: If specified final tax is Rs 50,000 and available prepaid credits Rs 35,000, remaining tax is Rs 15,000 before any other stated adjustments.
column4: The same values require Rs 85,000 remaining tax by adding the credits to final liability.

column2: Electronic filing of tax-return information with applicable verification requirements
column3: Uploading a return and completing required verification are distinct compliance steps.
column4: Uploading a return file always completes every verification requirement automatically.
